Vickman @stratton001 Introducing STYX — built at NEAR HACKATHON on @NEARProtocol to bring scoped spending, delivery verification, and owner-controlled payments to agent services. As agents take on more useful work, one question becomes harder to ignore: how do we let them coordinate services without giving them unrestricted control over our money? An agent completing a task and a service requesting payment are only parts of the process. Someone still needs to define the rules, check what was delivered, and decide whether that delivery deserves payment. That is the workflow we built with STYX. HOW IT WORKS The current use case is turning structured invoices into accounting CSV files. An owner prepares a job and defines its scope, spending cap, permitted service, recipient, expiry, and delivery requirements. STYX compares service quotes and connects the selected work to those rules. The delivery then goes through deterministic checks for source coverage, arithmetic, duplicates, uncertainty, and integrity. The owner can inspect the actual CSV and verification results before accepting the work. For the NEAR testnet flow, the owner reviews and signs the relevant wallet actions. Buyer-agent, provider, and verifier roles use separate identities; they do not receive the owner’s wallet keys. A verified result can proceed to owner-approved payment. Failed checks block acceptance, and a reservation can be released without paying the provider. WHAT WE HAVE WORKING • Structured JSON/CSV invoice processing. • Local parsing, with optional NEAR AI extraction behind explicit data-sharing and API-cost consent. • Owner-defined rules and spending caps. • Service quote comparison. • Downloadable CSV deliveries and source comparisons. • Separate buyer-agent, provider, verifier, and owner roles. • NEAR testnet escrow, reservation, delivery, verification, and payment flows. • Transaction reconciliation that checks final receipts and contract state after interrupted or uncertain submissions. • Completed testnet payment and reservation-release examples. WHY BUILD THIS ON NEAR? STYX uses NEAR testnet to record and enforce the agreement and settlement flow, while keeping invoice contents off-chain. The application connects the work people can inspect with the payment actions owners authorize. A wallet redirect alone is not treated as settlement: STYX reconciles the transaction and contract state before reporting confirmation. The broader idea is a reusable pattern for agent services: bounded authority, inspectable delivery evidence, and explicit owner control over payment. TRY IT WITHOUT A WALLET We also built a public sample workspace so anyone can explore the product immediately. You can load 30 fictional invoices, set a spending cap, compare quotes, inspect the generated CSV, accept a successful delivery, or try an arithmetic-failure case and release the reservation. Each visitor gets an isolated temporary workspace. Sample payments are clearly labelled simulations and do not send NEAR. Separate proof links show earlier, actual NEAR testnet transactions. WHERE WE ARE TODAY STYX is a working testnet pilot. Both configured service providers are currently STYX-operated, and the verifier runs on a trusted server. The checks establish consistency with the supplied invoice data; they do not prove invoice authenticity. Independent security review, broader user testing, and operational hardening remain ahead before commercial use. We would love feedback from NEAR builders, agent developers, and people who work with invoice processing: what evidence would you need before allowing an agent-assisted workflow to release payment? Victor @Viktor_ella_ Handing over a blockchain project should mean handing over the control that makes it run. You can give someone the code, the website and all the project files, but that does not automatically give them permission to manage the contracts. They might have everything except the ability to actually run the project. Introducing Writ. I built Writ at NEAR HACKATHON to turn supported project permissions into transferable digital keys. Those keys are NFTs. But instead of only displaying a picture, they let their holders do something. Here’s a simple example. Ada manages an NFT collection. She creates a Writ and gives the account behind it permission to administer that collection. While Ada holds the Writ NFT, she can use its approved commands to issue collectibles. When Ben takes over, Ada sends him the NFT. Ben can now use those commands. Writ rejects Ada’s former-holder access, and temporary permissions granted under her ownership are cancelled. The collection stays where it is. The NFT changes hands, and control through Writ follows. No sale is required. A handover can simply be a transfer. And this goes beyond NFT collections. Writ currently supports five profiles: • Managing a compatible service contract • Exercising a DAO council seat • Administering a compatible NFT collection • Issuing tokens through a compatible token contract • Managing payouts from a native-NEAR treasury You can also lend someone a specific action with fixed limits and an expiry, without handing over the entire role. Before accepting a Writ, someone can inspect its holder, approved actions, temporary permissions, available funds and recorded history. Selling is optional. When a sale is used, a buyer can require declared conditions to pass before the purchase completes. Developers can also use Writ from their own applications through its standalone TypeScript SDK. The holder does not need to stay on Writ’s website to exercise the permission. The technical part: Each Writ has a dedicated NEAR account with no access keys. NEAR smart contracts check the NFT’s current holder before forwarding an approved command to the external application. Transferring the NFT updates that authorization and invalidates the previous ownership’s temporary permissions. Supported ownership roles also allow a verified hand-back into the holder’s own wallet. These are reviewed integrations with specific contract interfaces, rather than a promise to control every contract automatically. The attached demo shows the full journey using real transactions on NEAR Testnet: create, grant permission, use, lend, transfer, execute from another application and hand control back. The client supports both testnet and mainnet. Mainnet users can connect a compatible Writ deployment on their chosen network. olaniyi wahab @wahabolaniyi090 What happens when an AI agent you trusted with a budget starts hiring other agents and delegating financial authority? How do you make sure those agents don't spend beyond their limits, send funds to unauthorised addresses or pass more authority down the chain than they actually have? This is a problem we believe needs to be solved as autonomous agents become part of the economy. That's why we built ROOTBOUND at NEAR HACKATHON. ROOTBOUND is an on-chain financial control layer that gives autonomous agents the ability to delegate work and financial authority without losing control of the funds. Here's what it does: • Recursive delegation: A manager agent can create child agents and assign them budgets and permissions. Each child inherits restrictions from its parent and cannot grant more authority than it has. • Budget enforcement: Tracks available, reserved and spent funds to prevent over-allocation and unauthorised spending. • Recipient restrictions: Agents can only make payments within their approved recipient boundaries. • Expiry and revocation: Delegated permissions can expire or be revoked to prevent further authorised activity. • On-chain accountability: Financial rules and transaction activity are enforced and recorded through smart contracts. We built ROOTBOUND on NEAR, using on-chain infrastructure to make financial authority programmable, enforceable and transparent. The bigger idea is simple: autonomous agents should be able to work together, hire other agents and manage resources without having unrestricted access to funds. The goal isn't to limit what agents can do. It's to make sure their authority has clear boundaries. Delegate the work. Not unlimited control. Watch the demo to see ROOTBOUND in action. Frank Olien | Building arc @frank_olien123 reintroducing Leash. the full flow Last night I gave an AI agent $20 and a web page that told it to send everything to a scammer. It paid the invoice it was supposed to pay, 10 cents, and the contract threw out the rest. Then I hit it with everything I could think of. A forged account history. A scammer registered yesterday. A name one letter off from someone it trusts. A payment split into small pieces. A single payment over the cap. Ten attacks, ten refusals, each one a transaction you can open. $0.00 moved. None of that was the model being careful. The model was fooled every time. The money stayed because the rules are not in the prompt. Leash is a spending account for AI agents on NEAR, and I built it at NEAR HACKATHON. Here is the whole trick. The agent never holds your key. It holds a NEAR function-call key, which is a thing @NEARProtocol has had since day one: a key that can only call the methods you name on the contract you name. The Leash key can say pay, request and ask_more. That is the complete list. Move USDC directly, add a key, loosen its own limit: the protocol refuses before a line of my code runs. The contract takes it from there. You give each agent a daily cap, a per-payment cap, a list of who it may pay, a cooldown and an expiry. Inside that, it pays on its own and your chat shows the receipt. Outside it, the payment parks. Parked is where your phone comes in. The request arrives on my iPhone a few seconds later. I read it, Face ID, done. If I am not sure, I deny it from the Lock Screen without unlocking anything. If the agent genuinely needs more for a job, it does not fail silently and it does not try again smaller. It asks, with a reason, and I can give it a raise for a while. Before any first payment to a stranger, the agent also gets the facts: how old the account is, whether its code changed this week, whether the name looks like someone I already pay, and whether another Leash owner reported it. Two reports and it is refused for everyone. Revoke deletes the key. Pause stops every agent at once. Every payment, refusal and approval is on chain, and anyone can read my dashboard. It plugs into what you already use. One line for Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. One tap in the Claude app, where the payment card shows up right in the chat. Agents can pay APIs per request too, x402 style, no API key. All of it is open source and running on NEAR testnet. The attack above runs live on the site with a real model, and the button is yours to press. leash.frankolien.com github.com/frankolien/lea… I would love to hear what you would want an agent to be allowed to buy without asking you.
